stem: Consecutive optic atrophy occurs in:
Consecutive optic atrophy occurs in:
explanation_verbatim: Consecutive optic atrophy follows degenerative retinal diseases like retinitis pigmentosa, where retinal degeneration leads to secondary optic nerve atrophy. It differs from primary optic atrophy, which originates from optic nerve pathology.

stem: A pituitary adenoma produces:
A pituitary adenoma produces:
explanation_verbatim: A pituitary adenoma compresses the optic chiasm, where nasal fibers from both eyes cross, leading to bitemporal hemianopia (loss of temporal visual fields in both eyes).

stem: Unilateral dilated pupil is not caused by:
Unilateral dilated pupil is not caused by:
explanation_verbatim: Horner syndrome causes miosis (small pupil), not dilation. Dilated pupils result from third nerve palsy, ocular trauma, or exposure to anticholinergic agents like atropine.

stem: Afferent pupillary defect is seen in:
Afferent pupillary defect is seen in:
explanation_verbatim: An afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) occurs when the optic nerve is damaged, as in optic atrophy. The pupil constricts less when light is shone in the affected eye.

stem: A left optic tract lesion is manifested by:
A left optic tract lesion is manifested by:
explanation_verbatim: A left optic tract lesion affects the right visual fields of both eyes, producing right homonymous hemianopia.

stem: Marcus Gunn pupil is found in which condition?
Marcus Gunn pupil is found in which condition?
explanation_verbatim: A Marcus Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect) occurs in optic nerve lesions, such as compressive optic neuropathy. The affected eye shows reduced constriction to direct light.

What is the most common cause of this presentation?
A 55-year-old patient presents with ptosis, diplopia, and the eye deviated “down and out.” The pupil is dilated and non-reactive to light. What is the most common cause of this presentation?
explanation_verbatim: Aneurysm compressing the oculomotor nerve causes ptosis, “down and out” eye, and pupil dilation. This is an emergency due to risk of rupture and subarachnoid hemorrhage.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with ptosis, miosis, and enophthalmos. Which investigation should be done to identify the cause?
A 60-year-old man presents with ptosis, miosis, and enophthalmos. Which investigation should be done to identify the cause?
explanation_verbatim: This presentation suggests Horner syndrome, which may result from a lesion along the sympathetic pathway commonly due to apical lung (Pancoast) tumor. Therefore, MRI of the thorax is the best investigation to identify the underlying cause.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 45-year-old man presents with unilateral ptosis, anhidrosis, enophthalmos,
and anisocoria that is more apparent in dim lighting.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_verbatim:
Horner syndrome is characterized by ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis,
and enophthalmos. The anisocoria is more evident in dim light
because the affected pupil fails to dilate.

stem: An elderly patient presents with sudden visual loss, headache, jaw claudication, and scalp tenderness. Which investigation is most important to confirm the diagnosis?
An elderly patient presents with sudden visual loss, headache, jaw claudication, and scalp tenderness. Which investigation is most important to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation_verbatim: Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) presents with vision loss, jaw claudication, and scalp tenderness. ESR (and CRP) are crucial for diagnosis and should be checked immediately.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 50-year-old patient presents with severe headache, nausea, and projectile vomiting. On ophthalmologic examination, bilateral blurred disc margins are noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_verbatim: Bilateral blurred disc margins with symptoms of raised intracranial pressure indicate papilledema. It results from increased intracranial pressure causing optic disc swelling.

stem: Most common cause of bilateral abducent nerve palsy?
Most common cause of bilateral abducent nerve palsy?
explanation_verbatim: ↑ Intracranial pressure causes downward traction on both abducens nerves as they run along the clivus, leading to bilateral abducent nerve palsy. It's the most common cause due to the long intracranial course of CN VI.

stem: Cause of pinpoint pupil?
Cause of pinpoint pupil?
explanation_verbatim: Organophosphorus compounds inhibit acetylcholinesterase, leading to excess acetylcholine and constricted (pinpoint) pupils. Mydriatics and Horner syndrome cause dilated pupils instead.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 60-year-old man reports sudden, transient, painless loss of vision in one eye lasting a few minutes, which resolved spontaneously.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_verbatim: Amaurosis fugax is transient monocular vision loss caused by retinal ischemia, often from carotid artery emboli. Vision typically returns within minutes.

stem: A 65-year-old patient presents with sudden, painless, and persistent loss of vision in one eye. Fundus examination shows a pale retina with a swollen optic disc. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A 65-year-old patient presents with sudden, painless, and persistent loss of vision in one eye. Fundus examination shows a pale retina with a swollen optic disc. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_verbatim: This condition results from sudden interruption of blood supply to the optic nerve head, leading to a pale swollen disc and permanent vision loss. It is common in elderly patients with vascular risk factors.

stem: Which of the following is a condition characterized by tertiary syphilis with midbrain affection?
Which of the following is a condition characterized by tertiary syphilis with midbrain affection?
explanation_verbatim: Argyll-Robertson pupils → Tertiary syphilis with midbrain affection. It is bilateral (may be asymmetric). It is characterized by small irregular pupils with light-near dissociation. Investigations: serologic testing for syphilis and MRI of the brainstem.

stem: A 64-year-old man presented for evaluation of binocular horizontal diplopia that began 2 weeks earlier and was most bothersome when viewing at a distance. He noted that the diplopia was more prominent when he directed his gaze to the left but otherwise it was present “all the time.” He had a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and dyslipidemia. On examination, of the patient’s left eye showed esodeviation and did not fully abduct, the fundus examination was normal. What is your diagnosis?

A 64-year-old man presented for evaluation of binocular horizontal diplopia that began 2 weeks earlier and was most bothersome when viewing at a distance. He noted that the diplopia was more prominent when he directed his gaze to the left but otherwise it was present “all the time.” He had a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and dyslipidemia. On examination, of the patient’s left eye showed esodeviation and did not fully abduct, the fundus examination was normal. What is your diagnosis?
explanation_verbatim: Sixth nerve palsy causes horizontal diplopia and limited abduction due to lateral rectus weakness. It is often related to diabetes or hypertension.

45-year-old woman comes to the emergency center because of severe left sided headache and double vision that began the night before, immediately following vigorous exercise. As you examine her, she continues to complain of severe left-sided headache. Her neuro-ophthalmologic examination is normal, except that the left upper eyelid is ptotic; and the left pupil is dilated 3 mm more than the right and responds very poorly to light. Her motility looks grossly normal.What is your diagnosis?
explanation_verbatim: Ptosis with a dilated, poorly reactive pupil indicates parasympathetic involvement of the oculomotor (III) nerve. The normal motility suggests partial or early third nerve palsy, often due to aneurysm or vascular compression.

explanation_verbatim: Proptosis, lid retraction, and restricted upgaze with mild pain are typical of thyroid eye disease due to autoimmune inflammation of extraocular muscles. The sluggish pupil helps rule out isolated nerve palsy.
